title: Chapter LI

teacherSummary.text: Lydia and Wickham visit Longbourn, unashamed. Lydia boasts of being married and lets slip that Darcy attended her wedding.

vocabulary.definition: An artifice or trick in war for deceiving the enemy
vocabulary.context: “Not that I shall though,” she added to herself, as she finished the letter; “and my dear aunt, if you do not tell me in an honourable manner, I shall certainly be reduced to tricks and stratagems to find it out.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “stratagem”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth looked expressively at Lydia; but she, who never heard nor saw anything of which she chose to be insensible, gaily continued, “Oh! mamma, do the people hereabouts know I am married today?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “hereabouts”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Sourness and harshness to the taste
vocabulary.context: His countenance rather gained in austerity; and he scarcely opened his lips.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “austerity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The first meal in the day, or that which is eaten at the first meal
vocabulary.context: “Well, and so we breakfasted at ten as usual; I thought it would never be over; for, by the by, you are to understand, that my uncle and aunt were horrid unpleasant all the time I was with them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “breakfast”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: One who has a part in anything with an other
vocabulary.context: We shall be at Newcastle all the winter, and I dare say there will be some balls, and I will take care to get good partners for them all.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “partner”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Lydia was Lydia still; untamed, unabashed, wild, noisy, and fearless.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fearless”: -less (Old English -leas, "without"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of delivering a religious discourse
vocabulary.context: And there was my aunt, all the time I was dressing, preaching and talking away just as if she was reading a sermon.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “preaching”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The easy assurance of the young couple, indeed, was enough to provoke him.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “provoke”: pro- (Latin pro, "forward, for") + vok (Latin vocare, "to call"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth had not before believed him quite equal to such assurance; but she sat down, resolving within herself, to draw no limits in future to the impudence of an impudent man.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “impudent”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Toward a part or place before or in front
vocabulary.context: Her mother stepped forwards, embraced her, and welcomed her with rapture; gave her hand with an affectionate smile to Wickham, who followed his lady, and wished them both joy, with an alacrity which showed no doubt of their happiness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “forwards”: ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: A married woman outranked her unmarried sisters socially, which Lydia flaunts.

significance: The slip reveals Darcy's secret role.
discussionQuestions: What does Lydia's boasting show about her values?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

items.prompt: How do Lydia and Wickham behave?
Who does Lydia say attended her wedding?
What social privilege does Lydia flaunt?
How does Elizabeth respond to the slip?

options: Sourness and harshness to the taste
The first meal in the day, or that which is eaten at the first meal
An artifice or trick in war for deceiving the enemy

options: Sourness and harshness to the taste

answerKey.answer: An artifice or trick in war for deceiving the enemy

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter LI,” how does Austen show shameless return? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LI develops the idea of shameless return. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter LI to complicate the reader's understanding of shameless return. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of shameless return responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of shameless return. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter LI”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: Lydia’s voice was heard in the vestibule; the door was thrown open, and she ran into the room. Her mother stepped forwards, embraced her, and welcomed her with rapture; gave her hand with an affectionate smile to Wickham, who followed his lady, and wished them both joy, with an alacrity which showed no doubt of their happiness.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Plot
annotationFocus.lookFor: key events and the causes linking them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Lydia's boasting show about her values? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are stratagems, hereabouts, austerity, breakfasted, partners. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““Not that I shall though,” she added to herself, as she finished the letter; “and my dear aunt, if you do not tell me in an honourable manner, I shall certainly be reduced to tricks and stratagems to find it out.”” Webster's says: An artifice or trick in war for deceiving the enemy. Now the word history: “stratagem”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “hereabouts”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “austerity”: -ity (Latin -itas, "quality of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. A married woman outranked her unmarried sisters socially, which Lydia flaunts. Why does this chapter matter? The slip reveals Darcy's secret role. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to shameless return.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Lydia’s voice was heard in the vestibule; the door was thrown open, and she ran into the room. Her mother stepped forwards, embraced her, and welcomed her with rapture; gave her hand with an affectionate smile to Wickham, who followed his lady, and wished them both joy, with an alacrity which showed no doubt of their happiness.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter LI,” how does Austen show shameless return? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about shameless return, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes shameless return. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
